title: AI Compute and Trends
description: Understand the scale and pace of AI: compute, hardware, infrastructure, falling inference prices, capability diffusion, and the limits of trend forecasts.
caveat: Checked October 23, 2026. Adapted from Epoch AI research (CC BY); authors are credited in linked sources. Historical trends and dated forecasts describe specific datasets. Approximate numerical answers are sufficient. Drafted and independently reviewed by AI; no person has reviewed it.

units.title: Reading AI growth numbers
units.desc: Separate amounts, rates, growth factors and forecasts before interpreting headlines.

items.p: What does a training-compute estimate in FLOP measure?
items.x: A FLOP is one floating-point operation. A training-compute estimate sums operations over the run.
keys: Total floating-point operations
o: The number of floating-point operations performed
The number of floating-point operations per second
The amount of electricity consumed during training
The number of parameters stored in the model
ow: Operations per second are measured in FLOP/s.
Electricity use is measured in units such as kWh.
Parameter count describes model size; compute counts operations.

items.p: What does a chip specification in FLOP/s measure?
items.x: FLOP/s measures computing speed. To estimate total operations, multiply an achieved rate by the time it runs.
keys: Operations per second
o: An energy requirement per floating-point operation
A rate of floating-point operations per second
A total count of operations over a training run
A dollar cost for one hour of computation
ow: Energy per operation is an efficiency measure.
A total operation count is measured in FLOP.
A rental price is measured in dollars per chip-hour.

items.p: Hypothetical: a system sustains 10^15 FLOP/s for 1,000 seconds. How much computation does it perform?
items.x: Multiply the sustained rate by elapsed seconds: 10^15 × 10^3 = 10^18 FLOP. The time unit cancels.
keys: 10^18 FLOP
o: 10^15 FLOP
10^18 FLOP/s
10^18 FLOP
10^12 FLOP
ow: This ignores the 1,000 seconds of work.
Multiplying rate by time produces FLOP, with no per-second term.
Dividing by time gives the wrong quantity here.

items.p: Hypothetical: two identical clusters run for the same time, one at 25% of peak compute and one at 50%. How does their delivered training compute compare?
items.x: Holding hardware and duration fixed, delivered compute scales with utilization. Peak specifications alone do not establish how many operations a training run used.
keys: Twice as much at 50% utilization
o: The clusters deliver the same amount of compute
The 50% cluster delivers 25% more compute
The 50% cluster delivers four times as much compute
The 50% cluster delivers twice as much compute
ow: Equal peak hardware can deliver different actual throughput.
Utilization rises by 25 percentage points, but the ratio is 50/25 = 2.
The ratio is 50/25 = 2.

items.p: Why can a training run use much less compute than peak chip speed multiplied by elapsed time?
items.x: Real workloads face memory bottlenecks, network latency and other overhead. Epoch accounts for the gap by including utilization in hardware-based estimates.
keys: Memory or communication overhead lowers utilization
items.answer: Memory and communication delays can leave compute units waiting

o: Memory and communication delays can leave compute units waiting
Peak speed already averages over the workload's idle periods
Wall-clock training time counts arithmetic execution time alone
The chip count already corrects for communication overhead
ow: Peak specifications describe theoretical throughput under specified conditions.
Wall-clock time can include waiting for memory or communication.
Utilization needs separate treatment even when chip count is known.

items.p: A quantity grows to five times its original value in one year. What is its percentage increase?
items.x: A fivefold final value contains the original amount plus four more copies. Percentage increase is (5 - 1) × 100 = 400%.
keys: 400% increase
ow: A 500% increase produces a sixfold final value.
A 5% increase produces a factor of 1.05.
A 50% increase produces a factor of 1.5.

items.p: Hypothetical: training compute grows fivefold each year. What is the multiplier after two years?
items.x: Growth compounds: 5 × 5 = 25. A constant annual factor adds increasing absolute amounts as the starting base grows.
keys: 25-fold
o: 5-fold
125-fold
25-fold
10-fold
ow: This counts only one year of growth.
That is three years of fivefold growth.
Adding the annual factors does not compound them.

items.p: What does an increase of one order of magnitude mean?
items.x: One order of magnitude, often abbreviated OOM, is a factor of ten. Two orders of magnitude are a factor of 100.
keys: Factor of ten
o: A doubling of the quantity
A one-percentage-point increase in the quantity
An increase of one in the quantity
A tenfold increase in the quantity
ow: A doubling is about 0.30 orders of magnitude.
Orders of magnitude measure multiplicative scale.
Adding one differs from multiplying by ten.

items.p: Hypothetical: computing capacity doubles every six months. What annual growth factor does that imply?
items.x: There are two six-month periods in a year, so the annual factor is 2 × 2 = 4. Doubling times describe compounding growth.
keys: 4x per year
o: Fourfold per year
Twofold per year
Sixfold per year
Twelvefold per year
ow: This counts only one of the two doublings.
The number of months is not the growth factor.
Monthly intervals do not imply one doubling each month.

items.p: Why should an observed fivefold annual growth trend be used cautiously in a five-year forecast?
items.x: A fitted historical trend summarizes a period of evidence. Extending it assumes that constraints and incentives remain sufficiently similar.
keys: Historical growth can change as bottlenecks or incentives change
items.answer: Future bottlenecks or changed incentives can alter the growth rate

o: Compounding arithmetic adjusts automatically for future resource limits
Future bottlenecks or changed incentives can alter the growth rate
A larger starting base makes the next five years easier to predict
A confidence interval for the past rate includes every future disruption
ow: Compounding projects a rate; it does not model resource constraints.
A larger base does not establish that the rate will continue.
Uncertainty in a historical fit does not fully capture future structural changes.

units.title: Scaling frontier training
units.desc: Track the compute and money behind leading training runs, and distinguish them from development budgets.

items.p: In Epoch's dashboard checked October 2026, how fast has frontier language-model training compute grown since 2020?
items.x: Epoch estimates roughly 5x annually, with a 90% confidence interval of about 4x to 6x. This concerns frontier language-model training runs.
keys: About 5x annually since 2020 for frontier language models
o: About fivefold per decade
About 5% per year
About fivefold per year
About 50% per year
ow: The dashboard estimates an annual fivefold factor.
5% annual growth is 1.05x.
50% annual growth is 1.5x, considerably slower.

items.p: What does frontier training-compute growth tell you most directly?
items.x: The frontier trend concerns high-compute models. It does not directly measure the average model, fleet-wide electricity or employment.
keys: Compute used in leading training runs
o: How every deployed model's capability changes each year
How all AI chips' combined electricity use changes
How total industry training and inference compute changes
How compute used by leading individual training runs changes
ow: Compute and capability have different units and relationships.
Fleet-wide energy needs information about the broader hardware stock and its use.
The frontier trend concerns individual high-compute training runs.

items.p: Hypothetical: a training run uses twice as many identical chips for the same duration at the same utilization. What happens to total compute?
items.x: In the simplified accounting, compute equals chip count × peak rate × utilization × time. More chips raise compute proportionally when all other factors remain fixed.
keys: Total compute doubles
o: It doubles
It stays constant
It quadruples
It halves
ow: More chips perform more total work under these assumptions.
Only one factor doubles in this scenario.
The change increases available processing rather than reducing it.

items.p: Hypothetical: chip count triples and training duration doubles, with per-chip speed and utilization unchanged. How much does training compute grow?
items.x: Independent multiplicative factors compound: 3 × 2 = 6. Actual cluster expansions can also change utilization, which this hypothetical holds fixed.
keys: Sixfold
o: Ninefold
Sixfold
Fivefold
Threefold
ow: The duration doubles rather than triples.
Adding 3 and 2 misses their multiplicative effect.
This ignores the longer duration.

items.p: Name two ways to increase a training run's total compute while holding per-chip peak speed and utilization fixed.
items.x: More chips working in parallel and a longer run both add operations. Faster chips and higher utilization are additional levers when those assumptions are relaxed.
keys: More chips
Longer training duration
items.answer: Use more chips and train for longer

o: Train on more tokens while reducing chip-hours proportionally
Increase the number of separate runs while keeping this run fixed
Use more chips and train for longer
Use more parameters while keeping total hardware-hours fixed
ow: Reducing chip-hours reduces compute under the stated assumptions.
Other runs do not add operations to the individual run in this question.
Fixed chip-hours and fixed per-chip speed/utilization imply fixed compute.

items.p: In Epoch's dashboard checked October 2026, roughly how fast has the cost to train frontier language models grown since 2020?
items.x: The dashboard estimates 3.5x annually, with a 90% confidence interval of 2.8x to 4.4x. This is a historical estimate, not a commitment by developers.
keys: About 3.5x annually since 2020
o: About 3.5% per year
About 35-fold per year
About 3.5-fold per decade
About 3.5-fold per year
ow: 3.5% is a factor of 1.035, far smaller.
35x is ten times the estimated annual factor.
The estimate applies per year.

items.p: How can training compute grow faster than the dollar cost of training?
items.x: Improving price-performance allows a budget to buy more computation. Compute growth and spending growth can therefore differ.
keys: Improving compute per dollar
o: More operations can be purchased per dollar over time
Compute growth is measured after subtracting hardware improvements
The dollar estimate rises only when the chip count rises
Longer runs increase FLOP without increasing hardware time
ow: Training compute counts operations before adjusting for hardware economics.
Dollar cost can change with duration, utilization and prices too.
Longer runs consume more chip-time, which carries a cost.

items.p: A model's final-run compute bill includes chip rental and electricity. Which additional expense could make its total development budget larger?
items.x: Final-run compute cost covers a limited part of model development. Experiments, staffing and other development costs require separate accounting.
keys: Experiments or salaries outside final-run compute
o: The final run's operations multiplied by the same rental price again
Earlier experiments and researcher salaries
The final run's electricity already included in that compute bill
The final run's chip rental already included in that compute bill
ow: Repricing the same operations twice would double-count them.
An expense already included in the bill should not be added twice.
The stated rental bill already covers that final-run chip-time.

items.p: Why is buying an entire training cluster usually more expensive than the hardware cost allocated to a single training run?
items.x: An estimate of a run's hardware cost can allocate part of the equipment's lifetime expense to the time used. The upfront purchase and the allocated run cost answer different questions.
keys: A run uses only part of the hardware useful life
o: The purchase price should be charged in full to each run
The resale value should be added to the original purchase cost
The cluster can be used for multiple runs over its useful life
A run is allocated only electricity, with no share of equipment cost
ow: Charging the full purchase to every run repeatedly counts the same equipment.
Resale value can reduce net ownership cost rather than increase it.
Run-cost accounting can allocate part of the equipment cost as well as energy.

items.p: Why is a headline saying "this model cost 10 million dollars" hard to interpret without more detail?
items.x: Check what is included, the time period and whether the estimate uses rental prices or allocated ownership costs. Different scopes can produce valid but very different figures.
keys: Need the accounting scope of the cost estimate
items.answer: It may refer to a final run, total development, or infrastructure spending

o: It should be treated as the model's full development cost
It should be treated as the cluster's upfront purchase price
It should be treated as the model's annual inference bill
It may refer to a final run, total development, or infrastructure spending
ow: The headline alone does not establish that research and staffing are included.
A run-cost estimate can allocate only part of a cluster's lifetime cost.
Inference expenses need their own period and workload scope.

units.title: Hardware economics and bottlenecks
units.desc: Understand what better chip specifications buy, and where the real workload can fall short.

items.p: For chips purchased from Q1 2023 to Q4 2025, what annual gain in performance per dollar did Epoch estimate in August 2026?
items.x: Venkat Somala's Epoch analysis estimates 49% per year in constant 2025 dollars, with a 90% interval of 36% to 66%. It measures peak performance of chips sold.
keys: About 49% annually in constant 2025 dollars
o: About 49% per year
About 5% per year
About 490% per year
About 49-fold per year
ow: This is much smaller than the estimated gain.
490% growth is a factor of 5.9.
A 49% gain is a factor of 1.49.

items.p: In Epoch's 2026 chip price-performance analysis, what does the quarterly aggregate represent?
items.x: The figure reflects the mix of chips bought each quarter. Chips accounting for more spending have more influence on the aggregate.
keys: Combined peak performance sold divided by spending
o: The average model capability achieved per dollar of training
Total peak performance sold divided by total chip spending
The best available chip's performance per rental dollar
An equal-weighted average of each chip model's benchmark score
ow: Chip throughput differs from model capability.
The analysis uses purchase prices and the sales mix.
The aggregate is spending-weighted rather than one vote per chip model.

items.p: Why express a hardware price-performance trend in constant 2025 dollars?
items.x: Constant dollars adjust money values to a common purchasing-power baseline. This adjustment does not eliminate differences in transaction prices or workload performance.
keys: Adjust for inflation
o: To convert peak specifications into measured workload throughput
To include all future electricity costs in the purchase price
To remove inflation's effect on the purchasing-power comparison
To ensure every customer paid the same chip price
ow: Inflation adjustment changes the monetary denominator.
Future operating costs require separate accounting.
Customers can still pay different prices.

items.p: How can a newer chip cost more while offering better performance per dollar?
items.x: Performance per dollar is a ratio. A higher-priced chip improves that ratio if performance increases even more in proportional terms.
keys: Performance grows proportionally faster than price
o: Its price rises by a larger proportion than its performance
Its performance and price rise by the same proportion
Its price rises while performance stays the same
Its performance rises by a larger proportion than its price
ow: That would worsen performance per dollar.
Equal proportional changes leave the ratio unchanged.
A higher price for equal performance worsens the ratio.

items.p: A newer GPU has better peak arithmetic per dollar but unchanged memory bandwidth. Why might it provide little speedup on a memory-bound workload?
items.x: A memory-bound workload waits for data rather than arithmetic units. Better peak arithmetic per dollar helps less when memory bandwidth remains the limiting resource.
keys: Unchanged memory bandwidth leaves the workload bottleneck in place
items.answer: Data delivery can remain the bottleneck, leaving the extra arithmetic capacity underused

o: Data delivery can remain the bottleneck, leaving the extra arithmetic capacity underused
The unchanged memory bandwidth means its arithmetic units cannot perform any operations
A better arithmetic-per-dollar ratio guarantees an equal improvement in memory transfer speed
A higher peak arithmetic rate measures the amount of data that fits in GPU memory
ow: Unchanged bandwidth can limit speedup without preventing useful work.
Arithmetic throughput and memory transfer speed are separate specifications.
Memory capacity is distinct from arithmetic rate.

items.p: What does GPU memory bandwidth describe?
items.x: Bandwidth is a data-transfer rate. Memory capacity is the amount that fits, while compute throughput is the rate of arithmetic work.
keys: Data-transfer rate between memory and computation
o: How many arithmetic operations the GPU can perform each second
How quickly data can move between GPU memory and processing units
How much data can be stored in GPU memory at once
How quickly chips exchange data over their network links
ow: Arithmetic operations per second measure compute throughput.
The amount that fits is memory capacity.
Inter-chip network bandwidth is distinct from GPU memory bandwidth.

items.p: A workload spends most of its time waiting for data from GPU memory. Which upgrade most directly targets that bottleneck?
items.x: A memory-bound workload needs data delivered faster. More arithmetic capacity helps less when arithmetic units already wait for memory.
keys: Increase memory bandwidth
o: More memory capacity with unchanged transfer speed
Higher inter-chip bandwidth when no chip exchange is required
Higher memory bandwidth
More arithmetic units with unchanged memory bandwidth
ow: Extra capacity holds more data but does not necessarily move it faster.
That upgrade targets communication between chips rather than the stated bottleneck.
Additional arithmetic units do not directly increase memory data supply.

items.p: Why check number format when comparing two chips' published FLOP/s?
items.x: A chip may perform more operations per second at lower precision. Comparisons should state the format and whether the workload can use it.
keys: Throughput depends on number format
o: Every format listed for a chip has the same peak throughput
The lowest-precision specification is usable by every workload
One FLOP/s figure directly measures the model's output accuracy
Peak operation rates can differ between formats such as FP8 and FP16
ow: Hardware can execute formats at different rates.
A workload may require higher precision or lack support for that format.
Chip throughput and model output quality are different quantities.

items.p: What does a higher FLOP/s-per-watt figure mean under the same specification conditions?
items.x: FLOP/s divided by watts measures operations per unit of energy. Actual system efficiency still depends on utilization and overhead.
keys: More operations per unit of energy
o: More arithmetic throughput for each watt of power
Less upfront spending for each operation per second
More arithmetic throughput at the same total electricity bill
More arithmetic throughput per gigabyte of GPU memory
ow: Purchase-price efficiency uses a dollar denominator.
The electricity bill also depends on operating time and electricity prices.
That is a throughput-to-memory-capacity ratio.

items.p: Why might doubling the chips in a training cluster deliver less than double the training throughput?
items.x: Chips in distributed training must coordinate and exchange data. A larger cluster can spend a greater share of time on communication.
keys: Communication overhead can lower utilization at scale
items.answer: Communication overhead can rise and lower utilization

o: Doubling the chips requires twice the duration for the same training run
Communication overhead can rise and lower utilization
Chip count already includes the slowdown from network communication
Per-chip peak speed alone determines total cluster throughput
ow: More chips do not inherently require longer duration for the same work.
Chip count measures installed hardware; utilization captures other losses.
Throughput also depends on chip count and achieved utilization.

units.title: Global chips and physical infrastructure
units.desc: Read global capacity estimates and the power, cost and construction constraints behind them.

items.p: According to Epoch's global AI chip estimate checked October 2026, roughly how often has computing capacity doubled since 2022?
items.x: Josh You and colleagues at Epoch estimate roughly a seven-month doubling time. The underlying chip-sales data are a proxy for available capacity, with deployment lags and retirement caveats.
keys: About every seven months since 2022
o: About every seven weeks
About every seventy months
About every seven months
About every seven years
ow: Seven weeks would imply much faster growth.
Seventy months would imply much slower growth.
The estimated doubling time is measured in months.

items.p: What does a fleet size reported in H100-equivalents primarily convey?
items.x: H100e is a hardware-capacity comparison using stated chip specifications. A fleet of other chip types can also be expressed in H100-equivalents.
keys: Capacity relative to an H100 reference
o: A physical count of NVIDIA H100 chips owned
A count of H100-sized servers regardless of chip type
Delivered throughput measured on the same real training workload
Computing capacity normalized to an NVIDIA H100 reference
ow: Equivalent capacity can come from several different chip types.
The reference is processing performance rather than a server count.
Specification-based equivalents do not directly measure delivered workload throughput.

items.p: Why can cumulative AI chip sales overstate computing capacity actually operating today?
items.x: Sales data help estimate the hardware stock, but installation takes time and older hardware can leave service. Operational capacity needs those adjustments.
keys: Deployment lags or retirement
o: Some sold chips await deployment or have been retired
Chip purchase prices must fall before computing capacity can increase
A chip sold to a cloud provider becomes capacity only when it is rented
A faster chip is counted as less capacity because fewer chips are needed
ow: More or faster chips can add capacity even if their prices rise.
A cloud provider can operate chips internally as well as rent them out.
Performance normalization gives a faster chip more equivalent capacity.

items.p: Why can global AI chip capacity grow while one developer's largest training run stays the same size?
items.x: The global stock is spread across owners and workloads. A single training run uses a particular allocation for a particular duration.
keys: Capacity can be allocated elsewhere or to other workloads
o: A larger global stock implies longer duration for every training run
Added capacity may go to other developers or to inference
A training run scales automatically with the global chip-sales total
Global capacity growth already corrects each lab's run for utilization
ow: Duration and chip allocation are separate choices.
A developer chooses and obtains a particular allocation.
A stock estimate does not determine a specific run's achieved utilization.

items.p: Why is installed computing capacity insufficient to estimate how much computation a fleet performs in a year?
items.x: Capacity is a potential rate of work. Annual computation also depends on uptime, workload allocation and the fraction of peak throughput achieved.
keys: Operating time
Achieved utilization
items.answer: You also need its operating time and achieved utilization

o: You need the chip count but can ignore per-chip performance
You need the peak specification but can ignore workload overhead
You also need its operating time and achieved utilization
You need the purchase price but can ignore operating time
ow: Different chip types deliver different performance.
Peak specifications need adjustment for achieved utilization.
Equipment price does not tell you how long it operates.

items.p: Hypothetical: a facility draws a constant 1 GW for 24 hours. How much energy does it use?
items.x: Energy equals power multiplied by time: 1 GW × 24 hours = 24 GWh. GW alone measures a rate, while GWh measures accumulated energy.

o: 1 GW per hour
24 GWh
1 GWh
24 GW

items.p: Why can total facility power exceed the IT power of an AI data center?
items.x: IT power covers computing equipment. Cooling and other infrastructure add to the total site load, so the two boundaries matter when comparing gigawatt claims.
keys: Cooling and other supporting equipment consume power
o: Facility power measures the chips alone without supporting equipment
IT power includes the entire electricity grid supplying the site
Cooling and supporting infrastructure also consume power
IT power measures electricity already accumulated during training

The grid supplies many loads outside this site's computing equipment.

items.x: Capacity describes what the site can support. Its actual draw varies with the equipment operating and how heavily it is used.

items.answer: Idle periods, maintenance and partial utilization reduce average draw

Capacity already averages over periods when equipment is switched off

units.title: The falling price of AI
units.desc: Track the cost of a fixed result, compare reasoning budgets, and distinguish cheap capability from cheap tokens.

items.p: Since 2023, how fast did the cost of a fixed benchmark performance level fall in Epoch's September 2026 study?
items.x: Emberson and Roodman estimated a 47% quarterly decline, about 13-fold annually, averaging five primary benchmarks. This is a historical estimate.
keys: About 13-fold per year; roughly an order of magnitude
o: About 50-fold per year
About 100-fold per year
About 13-fold per year
About 2-fold per year
ow: This is substantially faster than the headline average.
This is substantially faster than the headline average.
The study estimated a much faster average decline.

items.p: What should stay fixed when measuring how cheaply models can deliver the same capability?
items.x: An illustrative comparison asks what it costs to reach 80% on the same test at two dates. Changing the target confounds price and quality.
keys: Task and required performance
o: Task and required performance
The model and its release date
The token count and model size
The supplier and its list price
ow: A newer model can deliver the same result more cheaply.
Different token budgets can achieve the same result.
Holding a supplier fixed can miss cheaper alternatives.

items.p: Ignoring input costs and holding task success rate fixed, why can a model with a lower output-token price cost more per task?
items.x: Reasoning models make this distinction especially relevant. Compare spending for a required result.

items.answer: The model may need more tokens per task

The task must have become more difficult
The provider must charge more for inputs
The model may need more tokens per task

o: About 4 times cheaper
About 200 times cheaper
About 16 times cheaper
About 2 times cheaper

items.answer: Different budgets can change both spending and accuracy

A maximum-budget score summarizes its efficiency at every target
Different budgets can change both spending and accuracy

Training expenditure is a separate choice and is not mechanically raised by lower inference prices.

units.title: Software and capability measurement
units.desc: Separate algorithmic efficiency from hardware and learn what benchmark scores can support.

items.p: How fast did Epoch's December 2025 analysis estimate software reduced the training compute needed for the same measured capability?
items.x: Ho and colleagues inferred about a six-fold annual improvement from frontier models. This is an estimate conditional on their capability and compute model.
keys: About one-sixth as much compute each year
o: About one-sixth as much compute each year
About six percent less compute each year
About one-half as much compute each year
About one-hundredth as much compute each year
ow: A six-fold efficiency gain is much larger than a six-percent reduction.
The estimated efficiency improvement was faster than a two-fold annual gain.
The estimate was about six-fold, not one-hundred-fold.

items.p: Why can better training algorithms coexist with rising compute use for frontier model training?
items.x: Hypothetically, a six-fold efficiency gain lets a fixed budget reach a harder target. Developers can also increase that budget.
keys: Developers can spend the savings on higher capability
items.answer: Developers can spend the savings on higher capability

o: The estimate measures falling chip prices
The estimate includes increasingly difficult targets
The estimate caps feasible training compute
Developers can spend the savings on higher capability
ow: The cited software estimate concerns computation needed for a fixed measured capability.
Holding capability fixed is distinct from the targets developers choose in practice.
An efficiency estimate describes an input-output relation rather than a spending constraint.

items.p: Which change is evidence of training software efficiency, holding the model's capability target fixed?
items.x: Software efficiency concerns the computation required for a result. Hardware and power prices can change the money cost separately.
keys: Reaching the target with fewer arithmetic operations
o: Running the same operations on twice as many chips
Moving the same training run to a cheaper power grid
Reaching the target with fewer arithmetic operations
Buying the same operations at a lower chip price
ow: More parallel hardware may shorten elapsed time without reducing operations.
Cheaper electricity can lower cost without changing algorithmic compute needs.
Lower chip prices improve hardware economics.

items.p: What distinguishes inference scaling from pretraining scaling?
items.x: Extra answer-time reasoning or search can improve results. Its gains and costs must be measured for the task and budget.
keys: Inference scaling spends more compute while producing answers
o: Inference scaling spends more compute while producing answers
Inference scaling adds more examples to the pretraining set
Inference scaling enlarges the original training cluster
Inference scaling repeats the original pretraining run
ow: Adding pretraining examples changes the training process.
Cluster size alone says nothing about answer-time computation.
Repeating pretraining is still training.

items.p: Hypothetical: software cuts operations needed for a task in half, and hardware halves the cost per operation. What happens to compute cost for that task?
items.x: In this invented example, 1/2 times 1/2 equals 1/4. Multiply independent changes in separate factors, and check that estimates do not already include each other.
keys: It falls to one-quarter of its original level
o: It doubles relative to its original level
It falls to one-quarter of its original level
It falls to one-half of its original level
It falls to zero at the end of the year
ow: Both stipulated changes reduce cost.
That counts only one of the two independent improvements.
Multiplying two positive halves gives one-quarter.

items.p: Why can a benchmark near 100% stop revealing meaningful differences between improving models?
items.x: A saturated test has a ceiling effect. Harder evaluations can reveal differences it misses.
keys: The score has little remaining room to increase
o: The test's difficulty has stopped increasing
One score point means a fixed capability gain
The score has little remaining room to increase
A high test score establishes broad task equivalence
ow: A test's ceiling describes the evaluation rather than the full range of possible tasks.
Bounded benchmark scores are not a linear capability scale, especially near saturation.
A narrow test does not establish broad equivalence.

items.p: What is the main measurement advantage of combining benchmarks of different difficulties into ECI?
items.x: The Epoch Capabilities Index stitches together overlapping benchmark evidence. It remains a simplified statistical measure.
keys: Comparing capability as individual tests saturate
o: Comparing capability as individual tests saturate
Expressing all scores as percent correct
Giving each benchmark equal statistical weight
Measuring compute cost at a common performance target
ow: ECI is a fitted latent capability scale, not a shared percentage accuracy.
The framework models benchmark difficulty and discrimination.
A capability index and a cost-performance frontier answer different questions.

items.p: Hypothetical: one model has an ECI score of 160 and another 80. Does that establish that the first is twice as capable?
items.x: ECI is calibrated to reference models. A score difference can be informative without a score ratio representing a capability multiplier.
keys: No; ECI has an arbitrary zero and is not a ratio scale
items.answer: No; ECI has an arbitrary zero and is not a ratio scale

o: Yes; ECI ratios equal benchmark-accuracy ratios
Yes; zero ECI is calibrated as zero capability
No; ECI point differences are not comparable across the scale
No; ECI has an arbitrary zero and is not a ratio scale
ow: ECI and percentage accuracy are related nonlinearly through benchmark-specific curves.
The ECI zero is arbitrary, like its reference-model calibration.
ECI point differences can be informative even though ratios are not.

items.p: Why might a model with a lower general ECI score still be preferable for a particular coding workflow?
items.x: Test the workflow directly. Cost, reliability, and tools may affect the choice beyond a general capability ranking.
keys: Its strengths may align better with that specific workflow
o: General ECI weights tasks by commercial value
Its strengths may align better with that specific workflow
ECI uses pretraining size instead of evaluations
Lower ECI identifies lower reasoning-token use
ow: The index combines selected benchmarks rather than the full workplace task distribution.
ECI is fitted to benchmark performance.
An ECI score alone does not establish token use or cost.

items.p: A model improves on a coding benchmark. What additional evidence best supports a claim that it improves your team's productivity?
items.x: This evaluation recommendation follows from the gap between benchmark performance and useful work. Include human review and rework in the workflow measurement.
keys: Workflow tests of quality, total time, and rework
o: Workflow tests of quality, total time, and rework
A larger count of parameters in the model documentation
A lower API price without measuring task completion
A higher score on a second unrelated trivia benchmark
ow: Parameter count does not measure team productivity.
A lower price can coexist with slower or worse work.
Another benchmark can add context but does not directly test the workflow.

units.title: How capabilities spread
units.desc: Understand the open-weight frontier, domain gaps, and the practical limits of running models locally.

items.p: What makes a model open-weight in Epoch's model-accessibility classification?
items.x: Epoch uses open-weight for downloadable parameters. Code, data, and license permissions are separate dimensions of access.
keys: Its trained parameter values are available to download
o: Its API price is lower than competing providers' prices
Its full training dataset is available to download
Its trained parameter values are available to download
Anyone can chat with it through a public website
ow: Price and weight access are separate properties.
Training-data access is classified separately.
A chat service can keep model weights closed.

items.p: Why check the license before commercially deploying a downloadable AI model?
items.x: Epoch distinguishes unrestricted, restricted-use, and non-commercial open weights. Check the specific terms attached to the release.
keys: Downloadable weights can still have use restrictions
items.answer: Downloadable weights can still have use restrictions

o: Weight downloads permit unrestricted commerce
Licenses cover APIs rather than local weights
Downloadable weights can still have use restrictions
Local deployment exempts users from publisher licenses
ow: Availability of weights and permission for particular uses are separate.
Licenses can apply to use of downloaded model weights.
Running locally does not itself remove license conditions.

items.p: In Epoch's May 2026 analysis, roughly how far did the best open-weight models lag leading closed models on general ECI since January 2026?
items.x: Edwards and Emberson estimated a four-month average gap for this period. It is a dated comparison on general ECI.
keys: About four months
o: About two months on average
About four months on average
About nine months on average
About eighteen months on average
ow: That is shorter than the estimated four-month average.
That is longer than the estimated four-month average.
That is substantially longer than the estimated four-month average.

items.p: Hypothetical: open models trail the closed frontier by six months on one test. What does that lag describe?
items.x: A time lag compares when performance levels were reached. It depends on the metric, model set, and period.
keys: How long ago closed models reached comparable test performance
o: How long ago closed models reached comparable test performance
Time from model announcement to weight release
Extra pretraining time for an equally sized open model
Forecast time until today's best open model matches today's best closed one
ow: The lag compares capability frontiers across different releases, not a release schedule for one model.
It measures when scores were achieved rather than how long training took.
A measured historical lag is not a forecast of when the current performance gap will close.

items.p: Why should a general open-versus-closed model lag not be applied unchanged to every domain?
items.x: Epoch's October 16, 2026 topic update reports a six-to-seven-month Cyber ECI gap; its May general ECI analysis reported four months. These snapshots differ in date as well as domain.
keys: Model strengths and rates of diffusion differ by domain
o: A general index implies equal time lags in each domain
Open models are compared with a fixed closed reference
Time lags depend on release dates without performance evidence
Model strengths and rates of diffusion differ by domain
ow: An aggregate index does not establish one common gap for each domain.
Frontier comparisons track the best available models over time.
Estimating a lag requires both performance and dates.

items.p: In Epoch's August 2025 analysis, how far behind the frontier were leading models that fit on a single high-end consumer GPU?
items.x: Somala and Emberson compared selected knowledge, reasoning, and preference metrics. Their estimate depends on hardware and quantization assumptions.
keys: About six to twelve months
o: About six to twelve months on those metrics
About one to three months on those metrics
About eighteen to twenty-four months on those metrics
About three to four years on those metrics
ow: That is shorter than the six-to-twelve-month range reported.
That is longer than the six-to-twelve-month range reported.
That is substantially longer than the range reported.

items.p: Why is model weight size alone insufficient to decide whether an AI model fits in GPU memory?
items.x: The context-related KV cache and runtime overhead need space alongside weights. A longer context can increase memory demand.
keys: Context and runtime overhead also consume memory
items.answer: Context and runtime overhead also consume memory

o: The full training dataset must stay in memory
Checkpoint size includes the inference cache
Context and runtime overhead also consume memory
Parameter count fixes memory use without regard to precision
ow: Inference can run from trained weights without retaining the training corpus.
Context-related memory is additional to the checkpoint weights.
Bits per weight also affect how much memory the weights require.

items.p: What does weight quantization principally trade when making a model easier to fit on local hardware?
items.x: Lower precision reduces weight storage; aggressive quantization can harm output quality. Evaluate the chosen quantization on the intended tasks.
keys: Lower numerical precision for a smaller memory footprint
o: Removing whole model layers to reduce the parameter count
Lower numerical precision for a smaller memory footprint
Keeping weight precision fixed while shortening the prompt
Moving the same full-precision weights into CPU memory
ow: Layer removal changes architecture or parameter count; weight quantization changes representation.
Shorter prompts can reduce context memory but do not quantize weights.
Offloading moves storage rather than lowering weight precision.

items.p: Why can the frontier of all open-weight models differ from the frontier runnable on one consumer GPU?
items.x: Open-weight access describes availability. Local feasibility also depends on model size, precision, context, and hardware.
keys: Some downloadable models require more memory than that GPU has
o: The general open frontier uses the same single-GPU limit
Some downloadable models require more memory than that GPU has
Downloadability establishes a model fits on a consumer GPU
An API-hosted model runs in the client device's memory
ow: The frontier of all open models includes releases beyond the single-GPU size constraint.
Downloading a checkpoint does not establish that it fits in GPU memory.
A hosted service runs the model on server hardware rather than the client.

items.p: Why might a local model's historical benchmark lag understate its lag on practical tasks?
items.x: Epoch flags possible benchmark optimization among smaller models. A practical deployment still needs evaluation on its own workload.
keys: The small model may be optimized especially for those tests
o: The small model may be optimized especially for those tests
A benchmark score already averages the model's performance over the full range of real tasks
The measured release-date gap includes the time a user spends configuring local inference
The hardware memory filter directly measures response reliability on workplace tasks
ow: Selected benchmarks provide limited coverage rather than an exhaustive task average.
The release-date performance comparison does not include each user's setup time.
A model fitting in memory does not establish its task reliability.

units.title: Limits and uncertain futures
units.desc: Distinguish a constrained input from a ceiling on progress, and keep scenarios separate from forecasts.

items.p: What order of magnitude did Epoch's 2024 study give for the effective stock of human-generated public text for training?
items.x: Villalobos and colleagues estimated around 300 trillion tokens after quality and repetition adjustments. It is a modeled effective stock, not a raw count of every online word.
keys: Hundreds of trillions of tokens
o: Hundreds of millions of tokens
Hundreds of quadrillions of tokens
Hundreds of trillions of tokens
Hundreds of billions of tokens
ow: This is about six orders of magnitude smaller.
This is about three orders of magnitude larger.
This is about three orders of magnitude smaller.

items.p: What did Epoch's 2024 forecast say could happen between 2026 and 2032 if LLM development trends continued?
items.x: The forecast describes a potential bottleneck in public human text scaling. It is conditional on the development trajectory.
keys: Datasets could approach the public human text stock
o: The annual flow of new public text could fall to zero
Datasets could approach the public human text stock
Global computer storage could fill with AI training datasets
Public text could cease to be useful for training smaller models
ow: The forecast compares growing dataset sizes with a finite stock, not a halt in new writing.
The limiting quantity is useful public human text, not total storage hardware.
A scaling bottleneck does not remove the usefulness of existing data for smaller runs.

items.p: Why adjust a public text stock estimate for both quality and repetition?
items.x: Effective stock accounts for filtering and the value of multiple passes. A raw web-size estimate answers a different question.
keys: Useful learning signal differs from the raw count of tokens
o: A repeated training pass contributes the same information as an equal amount of new text
Filtering low-quality text and repeating useful text cancel exactly in every dataset
Useful learning signal differs from the raw count of tokens
The number of bytes stored is already a quality-adjusted measure of learning value
ow: Further passes can help but have diminishing returns compared with fresh data.
The net adjustment must be estimated; these effects need not cancel.
Storage size does not by itself measure training usefulness.

items.p: Name one way AI progress might continue if public human text can no longer provide larger training datasets.
items.x: Other possibilities include learning from richer modalities and improving data efficiency. These are possible responses, not guarantees that the bottleneck is solved.
keys: One valid route: synthetic data, transfer from other modalities, or data efficiency
items.answer: Examples: synthetic training data with quality checks; transfer from data-rich domains; improved data efficiency. Any one is sufficient.

o: Increase the tokenizer's token count without adding underlying information
Treat additional copies of the same examples as equally valuable new data
Use a larger model as a substitute for evaluating the training data's usefulness
Use synthetic training data with appropriate quality checks
ow: Changing tokenization does not by itself add information or solve data scarcity.
Repetition can help but is not indefinitely equivalent to fresh examples.
More parameters alone do not establish a new source of useful training signal.

items.p: Does training one model on a text dataset prevent another developer from training on the same text?
items.x: Data depletion in this context means limited new training signal for further scaling. It does not mean the text disappears after a run.
keys: No; the text remains reusable subject to access and permissions
o: Yes; the estimated data stock is a total allowance shared across all developers' runs
Yes; an earlier model's training makes the same examples unavailable for later runs
No; repeated exposure provides as much new signal as fresh examples
No; the text remains reusable subject to access and permissions
ow: The stock is available information, not an allowance allocated among all training runs.
Training on a dataset does not by itself make it unavailable to another run.
Reuse is possible, but repeated exposure can have diminishing returns.

lessons.title: How far can trends take us?

items.p: In Epoch's July 2025 model, roughly where was the threshold beyond which frontier training runs may become economically inefficient?
items.x: Emberson and Edelman's model suggested runs beyond about nine months may lose to runs started later with better technology. This is an economic estimate.
keys: About nine months
o: About nine months
About three months
About eighteen months
About three years
ow: Three months is below the model's approximate nine-month threshold.
Eighteen months is above the model's approximate nine-month threshold.
Three years is well above the model's approximate nine-month threshold.

items.p: Why can a very long AI training run lose economically to a run started later?
items.x: Rapid technological progress creates an opportunity cost to committing to an older training setup for too long.
keys: Later runs can use better hardware and methods
items.answer: Later runs can use better hardware and methods

o: Longer training reduces model accuracy
Later runs can use better hardware and methods
Depreciation imposes a fixed stopping date
Longer elapsed time raises operations needed for a fixed capability
ow: The argument compares runs benefiting from technological progress; it does not assume accuracy falls with time.
Depreciation alone does not establish this stopping rule.
Elapsed time alone does not change the algorithmic operations required for a fixed target.

items.p: If economically sensible training durations stop growing, how could total training compute still increase?
items.x: Larger or faster clusters can raise operations per second. Epoch also discusses distributing training across multiple clusters as a possible response.
keys: Use more effective computing capacity during each run
o: Improve software while keeping operations unchanged
Use more effective computing capacity during each run
More tokens with the same operation rate and duration
Buy cheaper chips with the same speed and quantity
ow: That improves capability per operation but does not increase the operation count itself.
Token count alone does not override the stipulated fixed operation rate and duration.
Cheaper chips lower expenditure without increasing compute when speed and count stay fixed.

items.p: Hypothetical: frontier training compute grows five-fold annually for three years. What follows under that assumption?
items.x: This scenario is arithmetic, not a forecast. Its implications depend on resource constraints and how additional compute translates into useful capability.
keys: 125-fold compute increase
Conditional on five-fold annual growth for three years
o: A fifteen-fold increase in compute, if the growth rate continues
A 125-fold increase in benchmark accuracy, if the compute trend continues
A 125-fold increase in compute, conditional on the growth continuing
A five-fold increase in compute, averaged across the three years
ow: Three fivefold factors multiply rather than add.
A compute multiplier is not a benchmark-accuracy multiplier.
Five-fold is the stipulated one-year factor, not the cumulative three-year factor.

items.p: Why does a historical trend in AI compute or benchmark scores fail to determine a precise AGI arrival date by itself?
items.x: A timeline needs an explicit target, a mapping from evidence to that target, and assumptions about future conditions. Historical trends inform those assumptions.
keys: Uncertain links from compute and scores to useful capability
o: Compute growth maps proportionally to workplace output
An ECI cutoff defines AGI without a task specification
A historical confidence interval captures all future breakthroughs
Uncertain links from compute and scores to useful capability
ow: The mapping from computation to output is empirical and need not be proportional.
A claim about full automation requires a defined capability target and supporting evaluation.
A historical fit does not exhaust uncertainty about future mechanisms and bottlenecks.
